title: Applied Econometrics Exercises in R
text:
Preface
This book contains R solutions to exercises from Applied Econometrics by Dimitrios Asteriou and Stephen G. Hall. Each chapter corresponds to a textbook chapter and walks through the data exploration, model building, and interpretation of results.

title: Applied Econometrics Exercises in R
text:
Tools
All exercises are solved using R with the tidyverse ecosystem, including:

tidyverse for data wrangling and visualization
broom for tidy model output
modelsummary for model comparison tables

title: 1  Multiple Regression — Questions
text: 1.1 Essay-Type Question

title: 1  Multiple Regression — Questions
text:
Download data for at least 30 stock prices and for the general stock-market index for the stock market of your choice. Using the logarithmic return formula, create the return series for each stock and the market index.
Calculate summary statistics for all stocks and for the market, as well as the correlation matrix of these returns. Comment on your results by referring to mean returns, volatilities, coefficients of skewness and kurtosis, and correlation coefficients.
For each stock, estimate the \(\beta\) coefficient as it is suggested by the CAPM. Summarize and display your results in a table in the text. Comment on the significance of \(\alpha\)s and \(\beta\)s and on the values of \(\beta\)s and \(R^2\)s in terms of what is expected a priori from the theoretical form of the CAPM.
From the results derived in 3, create the required series in order to estimate the SML of the CAPM. Test the relevant hypotheses. Are your results supportive of the CAPM model?
Graph the average returns against the estimated \(\beta\)s (this is a graph of the SML) and comment on your graph with respect to CAPM findings.
Estimate alternative versions with additional variables (such as squared terms of the obtained betas, and the standard deviation of the residuals). Comment on your results.
Compare your findings with those of other empirical studies on this topic.
Write an analytical report of all your analysis. This should include: (a) a short Introduction; (b) a short Literature Review; (c) a Data Set section; (d) an Empirical Results section; and (e) a Conclusions section. Discuss the validity of the CAPM, including references if you refer to any similar studies.

title: 1  Multiple Regression — Questions
text:
1.2 Exercise 4.1
The file health.xls contains data for the following variables:

birth_weight = the weight of infants after birth; when low this can put an infant at risk of illness
cig = number of cigarettes the mother was smoking during pregnancy
fam_inc = the income of the family; the higher the family income the better the access to prenatal care for the family in general

We would expect that the latter two variables affect birth_weight.

Run a regression that includes both variables and explain the signs of the coefficients.
Estimate a regression that includes only fam_inc, and comment on your results.
Estimate a regression that includes only cig and comment on your results.
Present all three regressions summarized in a table and comment on your results, especially by comparing the changes in the estimated effects and the \(R^2\) of the three different models. What does the F-statistic suggest about the joint significance of the explanatory variables in the multiple regression case?
Test the hypothesis that the effect of cig is two times greater than the respective effect of fam_inc, using the Wald test.

title: 1  Multiple Regression — Questions
text:
1.3 Exercise 4.2
Use the data from the file wage.wf1 and estimate an equation that includes as determinants of the logarithm of the wage rate the variables educ, exper and tenure.

Comment on your results.
Conduct a test of whether another year of general workforce experience (captured by exper) has the same effect on log(wage) as another year of education (captured by educ). State clearly your null and alternative hypotheses and your restricted and unrestricted models. Use the Wald test to check for that hypothesis.
Conduct a redundant variable test for the explanatory variable exper. Comment on your results.
Estimate a model with exper and educ only and then conduct an omitted variable test for tenure in the model. Comment on your results.

title: 1  Multiple Regression — Questions
text:
1.4 Exercise 4.3
Use the data in the file money_uk.wf1 to estimate the parameters \(\alpha\), \(\beta\) and \(\gamma\) in the equation below:
\[\ln(M/P)_t = \alpha + \beta \ln(Y_t) + \gamma R_t + u_t\]

Briefly outline the theory behind the aggregate demand for money. Relate your discussion to the specification of the equation given above. In particular, explain first the meaning of the dependent variable and then the interpretation of \(\beta\) and \(\gamma\).
Perform appropriate tests of significance on the estimated parameters to investigate each of the following propositions: (i) that the demand for money increases with the level of real income; (ii) the demand for money is income-elastic; and (iii) the demand for money is inversely related to the rate of interest.

title: 1  Multiple Regression — Questions
text:
1.5 Exercise 4.4
The file Cobb_Douglas_us.wf1 contains data for output (\(Y\)), labour (\(L\)) and stock of capital (\(K\)) for the United States. Estimate a Cobb–Douglas type regression equation and check for constant returns to scale using the Wald test.

title: 1  Multiple Regression — Questions
text:
1.6 Exercise 4.5
The Excel dataset MRW.xls contains data on real GDP per capita and related variables from the Penn World Table for a sample of 121 countries. This dataset was used to estimate growth equations by N. G. Mankiw, D. Romer and D. N. Weil, “A contribution to the empirics of economic growth”, Quarterly Journal of Economics, 1992.
The dataset contains 11 variables:







Variable
Description




number
a country identifier between 1 and 121


country
country name


n
dummy = 1 if country is in the non-oil sample


i
dummy = 1 if country is in the intermediate sample


o
dummy = 1 if country is in the OECD sample


rgdpw60
real GDP per working age population in 1960


rgdpw85
real GDP per working age population in 1985


gdpgrowth
average annual growth rate of real GDP per working age population (1960–1985)


popgrowth
average annual growth rate of working age population (1960–1985)


iy
real investment as share of real GDP, averaged 1960–85


school
% of working age population in secondary school




Create a suitable data frame for cross-sectional data for 121 observations.
Load all the relevant data.
Calculate and report summary statistics for the full sample and the relevant sub-samples (non-oil, intermediate, OECD) for all variables. Briefly discuss your results.
Do the necessary variable transformations before proceeding with regression analysis.
Reproduce the results reported in TABLE I: Estimation of the textbook Solow Model on page 414 of the paper.
Report your results and check if they are different from MRW. Run the regressions for each sub-sample.
Check the restriction imposed by MRW (i.e., that the coefficient of \(\ln(\text{pop}) = -\ln(\text{iy})\)). Report the necessary results of this test.
Take all the necessary steps to reproduce and report results for TABLE II: Estimation of the Augmented Solow Model. Report your results.
(Advanced): Gather the latest data from Penn World Tables and redo everything for the latest available data. Are your conclusions similar to what MRW concluded in their seminal paper? If not, why? What can this mean?

title: 2  Multicollinearity — Exercises
text:
2.1 Exercise 5.1
The file imports_uk_y.wf1 contains yearly data (1972–1997) for real imports (IMP), real gross domestic product (GDP) and the relative consumer price index (CPI) of domestic to foreign prices for the US economy. Use these data to estimate the following model:
\[\ln(\text{IMP})_t = \beta_1 + \beta_2 \ln(\text{GDP})_t + \beta_3 \ln(\text{CPI})_t + u_t\]
Check whether there is multicollinearity in the data. Calculate the correlation matrix of the variables and comment regarding the possibility of multicollinearity. Also, run the following additional regressions:
\[\ln(\text{IMP})_t = \beta_1 + \beta_2 \ln(\text{GDP})_t + u_t\]
\[\ln(\text{IMP})_t = \beta_1 + \beta_2 \ln(\text{CPI})_t + u_t\]
\[\ln(\text{GDP})_t = \beta_1 + \beta_2 \ln(\text{CPI})_t + u_t\]
What can you conclude about the nature of multicollinearity from these results?

title: 2  Multicollinearity — Exercises
text:
2.2 Exercise 5.2
The file imports_uk.wf1 contains quarterly observations of the variables mentioned in Exercise 5.1. Repeat Exercise 5.1 using the quarterly (higher frequency) data. Do your results change?

title: 2  Multicollinearity — Exercises
text:
2.3 Exercise 5.3
Use the data in the file money_uk02.wf1 to estimate the parameters \(\alpha\), \(\beta\) and \(\gamma\) in the equation below:
\[\ln(M/P)_t = \alpha + \beta \ln(Y_t) + \gamma R_{1t} + u_t\]
where \(R_{1t}\) is the three-month treasury bill rate. For the rest of the variables the usual notation applies.

Use as an additional variable in the above equation \(R_{2t}\), which is the dollar interest rate.
Do you expect to find multicollinearity? Why?
Calculate the correlation matrix of all the variables. Which correlation coefficient is the largest?
Calculate auxiliary regressions and conclude whether the degree of multicollinearity in (a) is serious or not.

title: 2  Multicollinearity — Exercises
text:

The file cars.wf1 contains annual data from 1971–1986 (16 observations) for new cars sales in the US. The variables are defined as follows:

int_rate
interest rate (percentage)

Estimate a log-linear model that examines a demand function for new cars, including all explanatory variables as regressors. Discuss your results.
In the model estimated above, do you expect to face multicollinearity? Discuss why.
Check if there is indeed multicollinearity among the regressors. How will you do that? What are your conclusions?
Based on your answer above, now develop a more suitable model that avoids the problems of multicollinearity.

title: 3  Heteroskedasticity — Exercises
text:
3.1 Exercise 6.1
Use the data in the file houseprice.wf1 to estimate a model of:
\[\text{price}_i = \beta_1 + \beta_2 \text{sqfeet}_i + u_i\]
Check for heteroskedasticity using the White and the Goldfeld–Quandt tests. Obtain GLS estimates for the following assumptions: (a) \(\text{Var}(u_i) = \sigma^2 \text{sqfeet}_i\) and (b) \(\text{Var}(u_i) = \sigma^2 \text{sqfeet}_i^2\). Comment on the sensitivity of the estimates and their standard errors to the heteroskedastic specification. For each of the two cases, use both the White and the Goldfeld–Quandt tests to see whether heteroskedasticity has been eliminated.

title: 3  Heteroskedasticity — Exercises
text:
3.2 Exercise 6.2
Use the data in Greek_SME.wf1 to estimate the effect of size (proxied by number of employees) on the profit/sales ratio. Check whether the residuals in this equation are heteroskedastic by applying all the tests for detection of heteroskedasticity (both formal and informal) described in this chapter. If there is heteroskedasticity, obtain the White’s corrected standard error estimates and construct confidence intervals to find the differences between the simple OLS and the White’s estimates.

title: 3  Heteroskedasticity — Exercises
text:
3.3 Exercise 6.3
Use the data in police.wf1 to estimate the equation that relates the actual value of the current budget (Y) with the expected value of the budget (X). Check for heteroskedasticity in this regression equation with all the known tests described in this chapter.

title: 3  Heteroskedasticity — Exercises
text:
3.4 Exercise 6.4
The file sleep.xls contains data for 706 individuals concerning sleeping habits and possible determinants of sleeping time. Estimate the following regression equation:
\[\text{sleep} = b_0 + b_1 \text{totwrk} + b_2 \text{educ} + b_3 \text{age} + b_4 \text{yngkid} + b_5 \text{male} + u\]

Check whether there is evidence of heteroskedasticity.
Is the estimated variance of \(u\) higher for men than women?
Re-estimate the model, correcting for heteroskedasticity. Compare the results obtained from this method with the simple OLS estimation results that were initially obtained.

title: 3  Heteroskedasticity — Exercises
text:
3.5 Exercise 6.5
Use the data in the file houseprice.xls to estimate the following equation:
\[\text{price} = b_0 + b_1 \text{lotsize} + b_2 \text{sqrft} + b_3 \text{bdrms} + u\]

Check whether there is evidence of heteroskedasticity.
Re-estimate the equation but this time instead of price use log(price) as the dependent variable. Check for heteroskedasticity again. Is there any change in your conclusion in (a)?
What does this example suggest about heteroskedasticity and the transformation used for the dependent variable?

title: 4  Misspecification — Exercises
text:
4.1 Exercise 8.1
The file wages_01.wf1 contains data for monthly wage rates (measured in UK pounds) and IQ scores of a large number of City University graduates after five years of employment:

title: 4  Misspecification — Exercises
text:
Find summary statistics for the above-mentioned variables and discuss them.
Estimate a functional form that will show how a one-point increase in the IQ score will change the respective wage rate by a constant amount measured in UK pounds. What is the change in the wage rate for a ten-point increase in the IQ score?
Estimate a functional form that will show how a one-point increase in the IQ score will have a percentage change effect on the wage rate. What is the percentage change in the wage rate for a ten-point increase in the IQ score?
Use the Box–Cox transformation to decide which of the two models is more appropriate.

title: 4  Misspecification — Exercises
text:
4.2 Exercise 8.2
The file Costs.xlsx contains data for real costs (cost) and real production (prod) for a car industry for the last 15 years.

Estimate the following regression model:

\[C_t = \beta_0 + \beta_1 P_t + \beta_2 P_t^2 + \beta_3 P_t^3 + u_t\]
and discuss the results.

Check the hypothesis that the cost function is of second degree only.
Check the hypothesis that the cost function is linear.
Obtain and plot the marginal cost function.

title: 4  Misspecification — Exercises
text:
4.3 Exercise 8.3
The file CD.xlsx contains data for the variables Production (Y), Labour (X1) and Capital (X2) of a hypothetical industry.

Estimate the following Cobb–Douglas production function: \(Y_t = \beta_0 X_{1t}^{\beta_1} X_{2t}^{\beta_2}\)
Check statistically whether \(\beta_1 = 0\), \(\beta_2 = 0\) as well as the overall significance of the model.
Check whether the hypothesis of constant returns to scale is valid.
Calculate the average productivity of labour (APL) and the marginal productivity of labour (MPL) for the values (Y, X1, X2).
Assume that in (a) a researcher wrongfully omitted the Capital (X2) variable. Perform the Ramsey RESET test to check if the model is correctly specified without this variable.

title: 4  Misspecification — Exercises
text:
4.4 Exercise 8.4
The file OECD.xlsx contains data for income per capita (inc_pc) and consumption per capita (cons_pc) for the 25 OECD country-members for the year 2020.

Estimate the relationship between consumption per capita and income per capita using a linear model. Interpret the results.
Estimate the relationship between consumption per capita and income per capita using a log-linear model. Interpret the results.
Estimate the relationship between consumption per capita and income per capita using a linear-log model. Interpret the results.
Estimate the relationship between consumption per capita and income per capita using a double-log model. Interpret the results.
Compare the models estimated in (a) linear, and (d) double-log. Which one is better and why?

title: 5  Dummy Variables — Exercises
text:
5.1 Exercise 9.1
The file wage2.dum.xls contains the following cross-sectional data:
\[\log(\text{wage}) = \beta_0 + \beta_1 \text{black} + u\]
Interpret the results and discuss whether or not a person belonging in the Black ethnic minority receives on average a lower/higher salary.
\[\log(\text{wage}) = \beta_0 + \beta_1 \text{black} + \beta_2 \text{educ} + \beta_3 \text{exper} + \beta_4 \text{tenure} + u\]
Discuss your results. Has the coefficient for the dummy variable “black” changed substantially or not? What does this mean?
